title: Verdance private deployment network kickoff
next_steps: Redwood: share private deployment topology diagram and IP ranges (RDW-TOPO-V1)
Verdance: confirm list of on-prem egress IPs and preferred AWS account IDs
Schedule 60m network design workshop with Verdance infra team next week
action_items: Connor: produce recommended Transit Gateway config and sample CloudFormation - due 2027-01-27
Priya: provide permitted CIDR and desired region list (EU-only) - due 2027-01-24

summary: Initial technical kickoff to map Verdance constraints for a Redwood Private (VPC) deployment. Main concerns: EU-only data residency, private endpoints vs peering, egress IP management, SSO/KMS, and pilot timeline. Agreed to share topology and schedule a deeper network design workshop.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Alejandra (Redwood CSM), Eric (Verdance VP Eng), Priya (Verdance Head Cloud), Liam (Security), Sofia (Network)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll kick us off, i'm maya from redwood, and with me is connor, our solutions engineer, and alejandra who will help coordinate the pilot. how's everyone doing?
[00:15] Eric: good, yeah thanks, a lot to cover so appreciate the time.
[00:22] Priya: hi all, we had a quick pre-call, so we want to go deep on network topology, region gating, and egress, mainly.
[00:32] Connor: great, i'll try to map our typical private deployment options — we support private endpoint (aws privatelink style), vpc peering/transit gateway, and hybrid on-prem via site-to-site. we'll cover pros/cons.
[00:46] Liam: quick note up front — security + compliance is table stakes for us. we need SOC2 type II, KMS/HSM key control, and the ability to keep inference traffic confined to EU regions.
[00:58] Maya: totally, understood. our private offering can be deployed inside your VPCs in a region you control. we have controls for key management and audit logs.
[01:12] Sofia: for networking, our infra team prefers not to do VPC peering with third parties; they prefer PrivateLink endpoints or a Transit Gateway attachment. is that something you support?
[01:25] Connor: yes, both. private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) are a common pattern — we publish service names and you create endpoints in your VPC. Transit Gateway works too for multi-VPC topologies; we can provide a TGW attachment with route tables. pros/cons: PrivateLink limits cross-account routing but is simpler for isolation; TGW gives more flexibility but requires attachment planning.
[01:50] Eric: any constraints around NAT / egress? we have strict allowlists for outgoing IPs from our VPCs. if traffic to redwood still egresses to public endpoints we need stable IPs.
[02:05] Maya: good question. for private deployments we minimize public egress. when using PrivateLink it's all within AWS backbone. if you opt for routing to a redwood-managed subnet, we will provide egress IP ranges for outbound callbacks and telemetry.
[02:24] Priya: we need static egress IPs for outbound callbacks to our monitoring systems too — can you guarantee ranges and documentation?
[02:33] Connor: yes, we publish the egress ranges per deployment and we can reserve / document them. there may be a small window during failover when IPs shift, we can mitigate with BYO-eip for some patterns — i'll detail that.
[02:49] Liam: what about VPC endpoints in Azure? part of our stack is Azure for persistence — we don't want cross-cloud traffic.
[02:57] Connor: we have comparable patterns on Azure using private endpoints; if your compute is in Azure we'd typically run the redwood runtime in the same cloud/region. cross-cloud would increase latency and complexity.
[03:12] Eric: can you run in eu-west-1 only? we have data residency lock — no US regions.
[03:18] Maya: yes, we can schedule the private control plane to operate in eu-west-1 and ensure runtime nodes sit in EU-only AZs. we'll need to check any dependencies — some 3rd party metrics may be routed through other regions but we can avoid that.
[03:34] Priya: also, regarding IAM/SAML, we need SSO integration and RBAC mapping to our groups. how are users provisioned into the redwood console?
[03:45] Alejandra: we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and role-based access. you can map your groups to Redwood roles. we'll share our SSO docs.
[03:56] Liam: KMS — we have a customer-managed CMK requirement. Can we bring our own key to encrypt model artifacts and logs?
[04:05] Connor: yes, BYOK is supported for Private. We integrate with your KMS — in AWS that would be a customer-managed CMK; for HSM we can integrate via CloudHSM or bring-your-own connectors depending on your setup.
[04:20] Sofia: networking detail — if we go with TGW, we want to avoid overlapping CIDRs. our infra team wants exact CIDR ranges you need from us and any IPs you'll advertise.
[04:32] Maya: absolutely, we'll provide a recommended CIDR matrix. connor, can you outline the minimal subnets and route table entries now?
[04:40] Connor: sure — typically we need two /24s per AZ: one for control plane, one for runtime (or a single /23 if you prefer). For TGW attachments we'll ask for a static route to the attachment with specific prefix lists. We'll send a CFN template.
[04:59] Priya: do you require public egress to fetch model updates or can those be pulled from private endpoints?
[05:08] Connor: model pulls can be configured to come from an internal artifact repository if you host it, or we can replicate artifacts into your S3 with VPC endpoint access. we prefer minimizing public access for model downloads.
[05:22] Eric: great. timeline — we want a pilot in 4 weeks if possible, low-volume. what's typical for Redwood private pilot?
[05:31] Maya: pilots are often 2–6 weeks. first week is network setup and connectivity validation, week two is model onboarding and smoke runs, then a couple weeks of load/quality checks. 4 weeks is doable if we lock the network details quickly.
[05:45] Liam: remediation: if you failover to another region, we need to be notified and ensure no data leaves EU. is automated failover to non-EU regions a risk?
[05:58] Connor: for your account we can disable cross-region failover. our default is to use nearest healthy region but it's configurable per account and we can set region constraints to EU-only.
[06:11] Sofia: what about private DNS? we use split-horizon DNS internally. how would private endpoints resolve?
[06:19] Connor: with PrivateLink you can set up private DNS entries so the service name resolves to the endpoint in your VPC. for TGW, you'd typically manage route tables and an internal DNS zone. we can provide a sample zone file.
[06:33] Eric: any latency numbers you can share for EU-only deployments?
[06:38] Connor: latency depends on model size and instance type, but we have benchmarks: for medium LLMs in eu-west-1 typical p95 token latency is ~120-220ms depending on batching. for smaller models it's ~30-60ms. we'll share a performance matrix.
[06:56] Priya: is there any additional logging we need to enable for audit? we require immutable audit logs for at least 12 months.
[07:05] Alejandra: audit logs for requests and admin actions can be shipped to your S3/Logstore with retention controls. we can also push logs into your SIEM via private connectivity.
[07:18] Liam: encryption in flight — TLS is required and we need mTLS for admin plane if possible.
[07:26] Connor: TLS is default for data in flight. mTLS can be configured for the control plane connections — we'll document the cert exchange process.
[07:37] Sofia: ports — do you need outbound 443 only? or any other ports?
[07:43] Connor: 443 for HTTPS; for some internal telemetry we might use port 5222 or ephemeral ports if you run the dedicated agent, but we can keep everything on 443 if required. we'll note that in the topology doc.
[07:57] Eric: if we choose a PrivateLink pattern, is the service in our account or does Redwood create an endpoint service in your account?
[08:05] Connor: Redwood publishes an endpoint service in our account; you create an endpoint in yours and accept it. We can also do an account-to-account approach if you want us to spin resources in your account under a managed role for compliance reasons.
[08:21] Priya: managed role approach — would that allow us to keep logs and artifacts in our account?
[08:27] Maya: yes, managed role can be set up so that artifact S3, logs, and metrics are written into your account; we still operate the control plane but resources live in your tenancy. That model is common for larger customers.
[08:43] Liam: are there known gotchas for Transit Gateway NAT rules? we run strict egress inspection appliances.
[08:52] Connor: the main things are asymmetric routing and inspection appliances that drop traffic if source/destination mismatched. We'll provide guidance: ensure return path via TGW and, if you have an inspection proxy, whitelist our egress IPs. Using private endpoints avoids NAT in many cases.
[09:11] Sofia: IPv6 — do you support?
[09:14] Connor: currently primary support is IPv4; IPv6 is on the roadmap but not for pilots.
[09:21] Priya: billing and metering — for private, how is usage metered and invoiced? we need chargeback info.
[09:29] Maya: private deployments are billed on committed capacity (monthly) plus overage and data transfer fees. we provide token-level and per-route cost breakdowns in the console for chargeback. we'll share a sample invoice layout.
[09:45] Eric: we need a security review — can you share your SOC2 report and pen test summary?
[09:50] Alejandra: yes, we'll send SOC2 Type II and the redacted penetration test report. we'll also provide the compliance pack (KMS, certs, and so on).
[10:03] Liam: network ACLs — will you ask us to open specific ports in our NACLs?
[10:09] Connor: generally we recommend security groups at endpoint level; NACLs usually only need port 443 allowed outbound. we'll specify exact entries.
[10:18] Priya: do you support multiple AZs for runtime for HA?
[10:22] Connor: yes, we recommend multi-AZ for production; pilots can be single-AZ. We'll need subnets in each AZ.
[10:33] Eric: how do upgrades/patching work? we need maintenance windows.
[10:38] Maya: we coordinate maintenance windows. For private deployments we offer more control — you can approve upgrades, and we have automatic and manual rollout options.
[10:50] Sofia: Service accounts — how do we authenticate internal services to call the redwood runtime?
[10:56] Connor: we use API keys and support mTLS for service-to-service. You can also use short-lived tokens via your STS for tighter control.
[11:07] Eric: can we run classifier models privately (small models) on-prem to reduce egress and keep latency low?
[11:15] Connor: yes, for latency-sensitive small models we can run an on-prem runtime; that requires a connector and a lightweight runtime image that talks to control plane over private link. For inference-only local runs you can pin models.
[11:31] Priya: cost tradeoff — if we run on-prem for some workloads how does that affect support and SLAs?
[11:38] Maya: on-prem incurs additional setup and support fees and a different SLA. We'll outline differences in the SOW.
[11:48] Liam: incident response — how do you integrate with our pager/duty?
[11:52] Alejandra: we can push alerts to your PagerDuty, Slack, or email with severity mapping. We also provide customer-facing incident runbooks.
[12:04] Eric: ok, i'd like to dive deeper into the TGW vs PrivateLink decision for our architecture — can you do a quick pros/cons summary?
[12:12] Connor: sure — TGW: good for multi-VPC with complex routing, one attachment handles many VPCs, but you need to manage routing carefully and it can be more invasive. PrivateLink: best for strong isolation with per-service endpoints, easier firewall rules, no cross-account route propagation, but more endpoints to manage if you have many services. For EU-only and strict compliance, PrivateLink often gives the simplest security posture.
[12:39] Sofia: do you support endpoint service acceptance by automation? we prefer not to manually accept many endpoint connections.
[12:46] Connor: yes, we can automate via CloudFormation or use an owner-managed approach where we create endpoints in your account with a role. We'll provide templates.
[12:57] Priya: example artifacts — can you send topology diagrams and the CFN template now?
[13:02] Maya: we'll share RDW-TOPO-V1 diagram and a CFN/ARM equivalent. link: https://drive.company/verdance-redwood-topology-v1.png (placeholder).
[13:16] Eric: good. any limitations on throughput or bursts for the pilot?
[13:22] Connor: pilot sizing depends on instance types; for low-volume pilot we recommend 2 runtime nodes with autoscaling thresholds. we'll include recommended CPU/GPU types in the doc.
[13:36] Liam: do you have IP allowlist ranges for external admin access? we require admin access restricted to our corporate CIDR.
[13:45] Connor: admin plane can be restricted by IP and we support SAML + IP allowlisting. We'll include a sample security policy.
[13:56] Priya: do you do deep packet inspection or is traffic opaque?
[13:59] Connor: we don't inspect customer payloads — telemetry is limited and scrubbed. You control logs and we can route them to your SIEM for audit.
[14:12] Eric: let's talk about fallback scenarios — if one AZ or region becomes unavailable, what's the RTO and RPO?
[14:18] Maya: RTO/RPO depend on architecture. For multi-AZ deployments RTO is minutes for service restart; for cross-region failover it depends on data replication policies, but we can configure region-lock to avoid cross-region failover.
[14:33] Sofia: do you support BGP route propagation for on-prem peering?
[14:37] Connor: yes with VPN or Direct Connect we can exchange routes, have BGP sessions for dynamic routing. We'll outline how that integrates with TGW or transit.
[14:49] Priya: about legal and procurement — can you accept our standard DPAs and addendum for EU data?
[14:56] Maya: we commonly sign DPAs and have EU addendums. Legal can engage once technical acceptance is confirmed.
[15:08] Eric: scheduling a network workshop — let's target next Wednesday.
[15:12] Alejandra: i'll send a Doodle and propose Wed/Thu next week, 60–90m deep-dive with your infra folks.
[15:20] Priya: fine, please include our cloud ops and security.
[15:24] Maya: great. any other outstanding questions?
[15:28] Liam: one more — data retention: logs and model artifacts, unsure what retention policy we should set. We prefer 90 days for artifacts by default.
[15:36] Connor: we can set artifact retention and you can snapshot models to your S3 for long-term storage. We'll recommend 90 days for working artifacts.
[15:46] Sofia: also, who will run the initial connectivity test from our side?
[15:51] Alejandra: our onboarding engineer will coordinate with Sofia and run the connectivity checks, collect traceroutes and test requests.
[15:59] Eric: ok sounds good.
[16:02] Maya: to recap — redwood will: share RDW-TOPO-V1, CFN templates, egress IP ranges, SOC2 and compliance pack. verdance will: provide CIDRs, account IDs, list of required telemetry endpoints, and availability for next-week network workshop.
[16:19] Priya: agreed.
[16:22] Maya: any blockers to starting the pilot once we have that network info?
[16:27] Eric: none from engineering, legal needs to review DPA but that's post-tech.
[16:33] Maya: perfect. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule. thanks everyone.
[16:38] Eric: thanks.
[47:45] Call end: final wrap up and calendar invites to be sent.

Notes:
- Shared artifacts: RDW-TOPO-V1 diagram, CFN template, SOC2 pack (links shared in follow-up).
- Pilot target: 4 weeks; network workshop next week.

Action items (also in metadata):
- Connor: Transit Gateway config + CFN (due 2027-01-27)
- Priya: CIDRs, account IDs, region list (due 2027-01-24)
- Liam: compliance questionnaire (due 2027-01-25)

End of transcript.
